title: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary
hook: a verse said over a plate of food, where everything in the meal is Brahman
carry: the offering, the fire and the one who offers
tomorrow: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma handed down: the sun, Manu, Ikshvaku, a teaching lost and told again by one whose birth and action are divine. What did you pass on? Day nine hundred sixty-six, the end of a week.

Before the first bite, in some Hindu homes, someone says a line in Sanskrit over the plate. Brahmarpanam brahma havir. It comes from chapter four of the Gita, and it's an odd thing to say before dinner, because it's a verse about a fire sacrifice. The offering is Brahman. The thing offered is Brahman. It's poured into the fire, which is Brahman, by the one offering, who is Brahman. A meal, a fire, a giver, all one. Today, the middle of chapter four, and how a single act can be seen all the way through.
screen: `A LINE SAID OVER THE PLATE.` → `THE OFFERING IS BRAHMAN.` → `ONE ACT, SEEN ALL THE WAY THROUGH.`

segments.voice: A few verses before the meal verse, Krishna sets a puzzle. What is action, and what is inaction? Even the wise, he says, are confused about this. Then the answer: the one who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, is wise among people, and does all their work in yoga. Shankara reads this as seeing that the Self never acts, even while the body is busy. Ramanuja reads it as seeing knowledge of the self alive inside work done without attachment. Then Krishna describes such a person. Their acts have been burned in the fire of knowledge. They've let go of clinging to the fruit, they're always content, depending on nothing, and though they keep acting, they do nothing at all. And then the meal verse. Brahman is the offering, Brahman the oblation, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman. The one who sees Brahman in the act goes to Brahman. Here's what's happened to our word since chapter three began. In chapter three, karma was action you can't avoid, done as offering, turning the wheel. Then action done for the world, the way Janaka did it. Then action handed down through a chain of teachers, and taken up by God. And now, action seen so clearly that the doer, the deed and the fire turn out to be one thing. Later in the chapter Krishna says it plainly: as a kindled fire turns wood to ash, the fire of knowledge turns all actions to ash. Look back over the week. Tagore's flute, emptied and filled. God in the dust with the pathmaker. A mind waking into thought and action. And the Gita's long answer to Arjuna's complaint: you can't stop acting, so learn to see what acting is.
screen: `INACTION IN ACTION, ACTION IN INACTION.` · `ACTS BURNED IN THE FIRE OF KNOWLEDGE.` · `BRAHMAN OFFERS BRAHMAN INTO BRAHMAN.` · `THE WEEK: FLUTE, DUST, WHEEL, FIRE.` · then, large: `SEE THE ACT ALL THE WAY THROUGH.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring to mind the last thing you ate, or the next thing you will. Go through it the way the verse does. The food. The hands that will lift it. The hunger it goes into. The one who's eating. Don't try to believe anything about it. Just look at each part, slowly, and then at all of them together as one act. If you pray, you can say the verse's opening words, brahmarpanam brahma havir, or a grace from your own tradition. If not, simply rest in the whole act at once. The bell holds the time.
Karma. In chapter four, action seen so clearly that the offering, the fire and the one who offers are one, and the act itself turns to ash in the fire of knowledge.
Your line: the offering, the fire and the one who offers. Today, before one meal, pause long enough to see the food, the hands and the hunger as a single act. Day nine hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Some Hindu families and schools recite Gita 4.24, 'brahmarpanam brahma havir', as a grace before meals.

fork.setup: Krishna asks: what is action, and what is inaction? even the wise are confused. what does he say the wise one sees?
options: inaction in action, and action in inaction.
that action and inaction don't matter.
fork.reveal: the wise one sees inaction in action and action in inaction. Shankara reads it as the Self never acting; Ramanuja as knowledge of the self alive in unattached work.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: brahmarpanam, the offering is Brahman. The opening word of Gita 4.24.

trapdoor: what you thought: karma is what piles up from what you do.
what it means: in chapter four, actions can be burned in the fire of knowledge, and seen so clearly that the doer, the deed and the fire are one.
what a scholar hears: 4.18 read by Shankara as the actionless Self and by Ramanuja as self-knowledge inside karma yoga, and 4.24 lifted from the fire sacrifice into a grace before meals.
